This code was written by Steve Simon on 2024-10-29 and is placed in the public domain.

This program is split into two parts.

# --- Part 1

This section of the program reads data on admissions to an emergency room before, during, and after a full moon. Find more information in the [data dictionary][ref-moon-yaml].

[ref-moon-yaml]: https://github.com/pmean/data/blob/master/files/full-moon-er-admissions.yaml

## Datasets

-   er: original data from full-moon-er-admissions.txt
-   er1: re-ordered factors

## Models

-   m1: two-factor ANOVA using aov function

## Load the tidyverse library

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(broom)
library(tidyverse)
```

## Read the data and view a brief summary

```{r}
#| label: read-moon

er <- read_tsv(
  "../data/full-moon-er-admissions.txt",
  col_types="ccn",
  col_names=TRUE)
names(er) <- tolower(names(er))
glimpse(er)
```

#### Comments on the code

This is a tab delimited file. I changed all the variable names to all lowercase. That's one less thing opportunity for inconsistency errors.

## Reorder the category levels, 1

```{r}
#| label: reorder-moon

moon_levels <- c(
    "Before",
    "During",
    "After")


month_levels <- c(
    "Aug", "Sep", "Oct",
    "Nov", "Dec", "Jan",
    "Feb", "Mar", "Apr",
    "May", "Jun", "Jul")

er |>
  mutate(moon=factor(moon, levels=moon_levels)) |>
  mutate(month=factor(month, levels=month_levels)) -> er1
```

#### Comments on the code

If you let R order the categories, it will do it alphabetically. The factor function will place them in a more logical order.

Since the study started in August, it makes sense to order the months starting then. An alphabetical ordering (April, August, December, ..., September) makes no sense here. Starting the levels at the first month of the study (August) makes that month the reference category.

There are several ways to think about the proper ordering of the moon factor. One is to list them in the order before, during, and after. This makes the time before a full moon the reference category.

## Draw boxplot of admission versus moon

```{r}
#| label: boxplots-admission-vs-moon
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 2.0

er1 |>
  ggplot() +
    aes(x=admission, y=moon) +
	  geom_boxplot() +
	  labs(
	  	x="ER admissions per day",
	  	y="Moon phase",
	  	caption="Simon, 2024-11-02")
```

#### Interpretation of the output

Although there are a few outliers, I would not worry too much about the normality assumption. It also looks like heterogeneity would not be too much of a concern.

## Draw scatterplot of admission versus month

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot-admission-vs-month
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 6

er1 |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(admission, month) +
  geom_point(shape="circle open") +
	labs(
	 	x="ER admissions per day",
	 	y="Month",
	 	caption="Simon, 2024-11-02")
```

#### Comment on the code

Normally, I would use a boxplot here. But in this dataset, there are only three data points per month. A boxplot is a graphical display of five number summary (min, 25th percentle, 50th percentile, 75th percentile, and maximum) and makes little sense with three observations.

#### Interpretation of the output

Although there are some unusual patterns here, keep in mind that there are only three observations per month. It looks like later months, shown near the top of the graph, are larger than earlier months, shown near the bottom of the graph.

## Calculate average ER admissions versus moon

```{r}
#| label: by-moon

er1 |>
  group_by(moon) |>
  summarize(
    admission_mn=mean(admission),
    admission_sd=sd(admission),
    n=n())
```

#### Interpretation of the output

There is a slightly higher average admission rate and slightly more variation during a full moon.

## Calculate average ER admissions versus month

```{r}
#| label: by-month

er1 |>
  group_by(month) |>
  summarize(
    admission_mn=mean(admission),
    admission_sd=sd(admission),
    n=n())
```

#### Interpretation of the output

Er admissions are trending upward over time and there is some evidence of heterogeneity. Again, treat this with caution as there are only three observations per month.

## Analysis of variance

```{r}
#| label: anova

m1 <- aov(admission ~ moon + month, data=er1)
tidy(m1)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

There is a borderline, but statistically significant difference in average admission rates during different phases of the moon. There is a statistically significant difference in average admission rates between some of the months.

## Tukey post hoc test

```{r}
#| label: tukey

TukeyHSD(m1)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The interpretation here is tricky. Start by ignoring the Tukey post hoc intervals for months. There are just too many intervals and the focus is not on the months anyway.

There is the temptation to state that the average number of admissions jumps from the time before a full moon to the time during a full moon and that it falls back again to about the same level after a full moon. There is a statistically significant difference between the "before" and "during" groups, but it is borderline. The lower limit is just barely above zero. 
There is not a statistically significant difference between the "during" and "after" groups, but again the results are borderline. The upper limit is just barely above zero.

The only really definitive finding is that there is no statistically significant difference between the "before" and "after" groups.

# --- Part 2

This section of the program reads data on fruit fly longevity. Find more information in the [data dictionary][ref-fruitfly-yaml].

[ref-fruitfly-yaml]: https://github.com/pmean/data/blob/master/files/fruitfly.yaml

## Datasets

-   fly: original data from ../data/fruitfly.txt
-   fly1: subset appropriate for two factor ANOVA
-   fly2: convert type, partners to factors

## Models

-   m2: two-factor ANOVA using aov function
-   m3: two-factor ANOVA using lm function

## List the variable names

```{r}
#| label: variable-list

vlist <- c(
  "id",
  "partners",
  "type",
  "longevity",
  "thorax",
  "sleep")
```

#### Comments on the code

When a dataset does not have variables on the first line, you need to specify them in the code.

## Read the data and view a brief summary

```{r}
#| label: read-fly

fly <- read_table(
  "../data/fruitfly.txt",
  col_types="nnnnnn",
  col_names=vlist)

glimpse(fly)
```

## Create a subset of fruitfly dataset

```{r}
#| label: subset

fly |>
  filter(type != 9) ->fly1

fly1 |>
  mutate(
    partners=
      factor(
        partners, 
        levels=c(1,8))) |> 
  mutate(
    type=
      factor(
        type,
        levels=0:1, 
        labels=c("Pregnant", "Virgin")))-> fly2
```

#### Comments on the code

If you exclude the pure control group (No females), you can analyze the two factors, partners and type individually. Partners has two category levels, 1 for when one female was included in the cage and 8 for when eight females were included in the cage. Type also has two category levels, 0 for pregnant female fly/flies and 1 for virgin fly/flies. A male fly will not mate with a pregnant females, so you can think of this as a second level of controls. The two factors are crossed, meaning that every possible combination of partners and type has outcomes measured.

Notice that the two categorical variables, partners and type, are actually numbers rather than strings. To avoid having R treat these variables as if they were continuous, use the factor function.

## Draw boxplot of longevity by partners and type

```{r}
#| label: boxplots-partners-type
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig.height: 2.5

fly2 |>
  ggplot() +
	aes(
		x=longevity, 
		y=partners,
		fill=type) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
  	x="Lifespan in days",
  	y="Number of partners",
  	fill="Female fly type",
  	caption="Steve Simon, 2024-10-28, CC0")
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The lifespans tend to be quite a bit shorter in cages with 8 virgin females. There are no problems with the homogeneity and normality assumptions.

## Calculate average longevity by partners and type

```{r}
#| label: line-graph

fly2 |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(
    x=partners, 
    y=longevity, 
    color=type, 
    group=type) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_summary(fun=mean, geom="line") +
	labs(
		x="Number of partners",
		y="Lifespan in days",
		color="Female fly type",
		caption="Simon, 2026-11-10") 
```

#### Comments on the code

The [stat_summary function][ref-stat], part of the ggplot2 library and tidyverse, reduces the data using a summary statistic before applying a graphical element. In this code, the argument fun=mean computes a simple average and the geom="line" argument connects the means using a line.

[ref-stat]: https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/stat_summary.html

#### Interpretation of the output

This plot shows strong evidence of an interaction.

Male fruitflies do appear to have shorter average lifespans when sharing a cage with virgin females compared to pregnant females, but this effect is far stronger when the number of female fruitflies is eight rather than one.

The line for pregnant (sharing a cage with pregnant females) is close to flat, indicating that there is little impact of the number of pregnant females on average longevity.

```{r}
#| label: by-partners-and-type
#| message: false

fly2 |>
  group_by(type, partners) |>
  summarize(
    longevity_mn=mean(longevity),
    longevity_sd=sd(longevity),
    n=n()) -> fly_means
fly_means
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The means show the same pattern as noted above. The standard deviations are all roughly the same.

It will help later to note how much things change. The reference levels are type=pregnant and partners=1. This has a mean of 64.8. Switching from these reference categories to type=pregnant and partners=8 leads to a 1.4 day decline. Switching from these reference categories to type=virgin and partners=1 leads to an 8.0 day decline. Switching from these reference categories to type=virgin and partners=9 leads to a 26.1 day decline.

## Analysis of variance including the interaction

```{r}
#| label: anova-with-interaction

m2 <- aov(longevity ~ partners*type, data=fly2)
anova(m2)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

There is a statistically significant interaction between the number of female partners and the type of partners (pregnant or virgin). When you have an interaction, you do not normally interpret the individual categorical predictors.

## Using lm, 1

```{r}
#| label: lm-with-interactions-1

m3 <- lm(longevity ~ partners*type, data=fly2)
anova(m3)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The analysis of variance table is identical when using lm instead of aov.

## Using lm, 2

```{r}
#| label: lm-with-interactions-2

tidy(m3)
```

#### Interpretation of the output

The intercept is the estimated average with both categories each to the "zero" or reference level. In this case, the estimated average lifespan of flies in a cage with one pregnant female is 65 days.

The first slope coefficient (b1) represents the estimated average difference in lifespan between eight pregnant females and one pregnant females. In this case, switching from one pregnant female to eight pregnant females decreases the estimated average life span by a bit more than 1.4 days.

The second slope coefficient (b2) represents the estimated average difference in lifespan between one pregnant females and one virgin female. In this case, switching from one pregnant female to one virgin female decreases the estimated average life span by 8.0 days.

The third slope coefficient (b3) represents the interaction. It is a measure of how much shorter the average lifespan is with eight virgin females above and beyond the individual impact of eight versus one and virgin versus pregnant. If there were no interaction, you would expect the cage with 8 virgin partners to be 1 day shorter due to the eight partners plus an additional 8 days shorter due to the ability to mate for a total of 9.4 days shorter. But with eight virgin females, the deficit is much worse, 26.1 days worse, which is 16.6 days worse than what you would see without an interaction.
